EMI can lead to the obstruction or degradation of the performance of any electrical equipment by inducing unwanted currents and voltages in its circuitry.
Radiated emission testing is typically done in the frequency range of 30 MHz to 1 GHz, corresponding to wavelengths of 10 m to 0.3 m.
The GTEM cell is a tapered two-conductor transmission line with a characteristic impedance of 50Ω, which can be used for EMI emission testing from 0 Hz to 20 GHz.
The 1Ω method for conducted emission testing can provide accurate results up to the gigahertz range, but it becomes less feasible if the EUT has a large number of pins.

IEC 61000-4-2 is the internationally accepted standard for immunity testing of electronic devices against electrostatic discharge (ESD), specifying test voltage levels for both contact discharge and air discharge.

Reverberation chambers provide more accurate and reliable results for radiated immunity testing compared to anechoic chambers, as the EUT is subjected to an external field from all directions simultaneously.
Electromagnetic shielding, EMI filters, circuit topology modification, and spread spectrum techniques are some of the key EMI reduction methods discussed in the paper.

Performing pre-compliance EMI testing at each stage of product development can significantly reduce the chances of the product failing the final compliance tests, which are expensive and time-consuming.

Over-the-air (OTA) measurements can be used to indirectly assess the radiated emissions of MIMO systems by obtaining the 3D radiation patterns in an anechoic chamber and then combining them using a base station emulator and channel model.

The shielding effectiveness of a material can be calculated using an equation that relates the field strength inside and outside the shielding material, taking into account factors like antenna geometry and wave number.
EMI/EMC plays a crucial role in electronic engineering, but research and development in this area is still insufficient compared to other aspects of electronic engineering and product development.
The literature available for EMI/EMC is scattered, making it difficult for young researchers to fully understand the structure of this field.
Efforts to mitigate the effects of EMI on electronic systems began during World War II, with a focus on defense applications, and later expanded to civilian applications in the 1970s and 1980s.
Almost all electronic systems experience as well as cause interference due to various involuntary and voluntary man-made sources of EMI.
Conducted emission testing is done to estimate the noise generated due to sudden changes in voltage or current in the circuitry of the equipment, which can have a fatal effect on connected devices.
